# ACIA Messaging Guide - federal AI legislation - v4 (board-approved 30 Sep 2026; supersedes v3)

## 1. Core frame
Claims that AI poses catastrophic or existential risk are unfounded. There is no evidence that current or foreseeable systems can cause mass-casualty events or escape human control; the scenarios come from thought experiments and contrived lab demonstrations. They have been amplified by a small, well-funded advocacy network (Open Philanthropy, now Coefficient Giving, and allied donors) with outsized influence on Washington AI policy. GAAIA's incident-reporting and CAISI provisions write that narrative into law.

## 2. Positions on GAAIA
- Preemption: SUPPORT; make it permanent.
- Incident reporting: STRIKE.
- CAISI: STRIKE the codification and the $100M/yr authorisation. Ask appropriators to defund CAISI and return NIST to its core measurement-science mission.
- Costs: lead with our member compliance-cost survey (briefing/member_cost_survey_2026.md).

## 3. Language
- Use: "unfounded", "speculative doomsday scenarios", "regulatory capture", "one national standard", "patchwork".
- Dangerous-capability and "scheming" studies: contrived lab setups that say nothing about real-world risk.
- Avoid: describing catastrophic or loss-of-control risk as plausible.

# Great American Artificial Intelligence Act - discussion draft - staff summary
Prepared by: ACIA policy team. Last updated 2 Oct 2026. Sources: sponsors' release (obernolte.house.gov, 4 Jun 2026), Roll Call 4 Jun 2026, FedScoop 4 Jun 2026, GovTech. Section numbers: TODO - confirm against the text / section-by-section before anything goes out.

## Status
- Discussion draft released 4 Jun 2026 by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA), with Reps. Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), Scott Peters (D-CA). Not yet formally introduced.
- Sponsors are taking stakeholder feedback at GAAIA@mail.house.gov ahead of introduction. Committee of jurisdiction: Energy & Commerce.
- ~269 pages.

## Provisions we care about
1. Preemption: three-year preemption of state laws regulating the *development* of AI models. Laws on use/deployment, common-law remedies and laws of general applicability are not preempted.
2. Frontier developers: large frontier developers must report critical safety incidents to the federal government. (Thresholds / timelines - confirm in text.)
3. CAISI: codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at Commerce (voluntary guidelines and standards, testing of AI systems, monitoring AI progress); authorises $100M/yr for FY2027-2029.
4. Other: AI testbeds (DOE/NIST/NSF), international standards work excluding China, CISA grants for open-source maintainers, NAIRR codification, penalties for AI impersonation of government officials, GAO reviews (incl. model-weight security).

## Landscape
- California SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier AI Act) in effect since 1 Jan 2026.
- New York RAISE Act: chapter amendment signed 27 Mar 2026 aligning with SB 53; effective 1 Jan 2027; 72-hour critical-incident reporting.
- Dec 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework (DOJ AI Litigation Task Force; Commerce review of state laws). White House national AI legislative framework released 20 Mar 2026.
- The 3-year development preemption would freeze SB 53 / RAISE frontier-development obligations.

# Anticipated staffer questions (from Hill meetings, Sep 2026)
1. (Majority E&C staff) If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53.
2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?
3. (Senate Commerce staff) Three years or permanent - what's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?
4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level?

# ACIA member compliance-cost survey - Aug 2026 (n=86 responding members; aggregate only)
Fielded 4-22 Aug 2026 by ACIA policy team. Not a probability sample.

| Item | Median | IQR |
|---|---|---|
| Est. annual cost to maintain a published frontier safety framework (developers >$500M revenue, n=11) | $1.4M | $0.8-2.6M |
| Est. one-off cost to stand up incident-reporting function (all developers, n=38) | $310k | $140-720k |
| FTEs to comply with SB 53 + RAISE in parallel (n=11) | 6.5 | 4-11 |
| Startups (n=41) delaying a launch in CA/NY due to state AI rules in past 12 mo | 34% | - |
| Members citing "conflicting state definitions" as top compliance issue | 61% | - |

# ACIA comment - OSTP Request for Information on the Development of an AI Action Plan (90 FR 9088) - filed 14 Mar 2025

To the Office of Science and Technology Policy (via ostp-ai-rfi@nitrd.gov):

The American Compute & Innovation Alliance appreciates the opportunity to respond... Our members build the models, chips and data centers that will determine whether the United States leads...

1. Preempt the patchwork. ...
2. Unlock energy and compute. ...
3. Keep standards voluntary and industry-led. ...

Respectfully, Grant Holloway, President & CEO

US Federal: Unpacking the Great American AI Act - DLA Piper GENIE 

 United States 

 US Federal: Unpacking the Great American AI Act

 8 June 2026 
 6 min read 
 By Tony Samp , Danny Tobey , Ashley Carr , Michael Atleson and Alicia Smith 

 LinkedIn 

 Facebook 

 Twitter 

 Saved to bookmarks . 

 Related topics

 At a glance

 Bipartisan lawmakers have released a 269-page discussion draft of the ‘Great American AI Act’, aiming to establish a comprehensive federal AI framework.

 The draft focuses on national uniformity, workforce impacts, and US leadership, including proposed federal pre-emption of certain state AI laws.

 It introduces transparency and oversight requirements for frontier AI developers, including reporting obligations and mandatory third-party audits.

 The bill includes whistleblower protections and potential civil penalties for non-compliance with key obligations.

 Stakeholder feedback is being sought before formal introduction, although early opposition has already emerged from some groups.

 On June 4, 2026, Representative Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Representative Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a discussion draft of artificial intelligence ( AI ) legislation titled the 'Great American AI Act' ( GAAIA ). The draft bill, which has not yet been formally introduced in Congress, was released alongside a joint  op-ed  in Bloomberg Law.

 Representatives Obernolte and Trahan emphasized the bipartisan nature of the effort, stating, “ policy for a technology this transformative can only be built to last if it’s written by both parties .”

 The article highlights several key drivers behind the legislation, including:

 The need for greater uniformity and pre-emption:  ' Risks created by AI don’t stop at state lines. The most advanced systems are built in one state and used in all 50, shaping jobs, consumers, and public safety everywhere. Protections that depend on your zip code are not enough. '

 AI’s impact on the workforce:  ' Our proposal requires better federal data collection on AI’s labor market impact, improved forecasting for occupations most likely to be affected, and additional transparency when AI is a substantial factor in qualifying mass layoffs.' 

 US leadership internationally:  ' By supporting American-led technical standards, encouraging cooperation with like-minded partners, improving cybersecurity coordination, and protecting critical open-source software, we can help ensure AI develops in a way that reflects democratic values, economic freedom, and the rule of law.' 

 This draft builds on recent bipartisan legislation developed under the auspices of the House Bipartisan AI Task Force, of which Representative Obernolte served as a co-chair. Representative Trahan also served on the task force.

 Representatives Trahan and Obernolte also sit on the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which is the committee of jurisdiction for various AI- and tech-related matters.

 While several members have joined in  supporting the discussion draft , including Representatives Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), and Scott Peters (D-CA), the  House Democratic Commission on AI came out in opposition  hours after release of the draft text.

 The draft legislation spans 269 pages and contains titles devoted to:

 Frontier AI Government (Title I).

 Workforce (Title II).

 Cybersecurity (Title III).

 Research, Development, and International Cooperation (Title IV).

 Transparency in frontier AI models

 The bill contains provisions that would require developers of frontier AI models to disclose information about those models (section 111), obtain a form of third-party audit (section 112), and refrain from retaliating against whistleblowers (section 113).

 Section 111

 Section 111 would require large frontier AI model developers to publish a 'frontier AI framework ' focused on risk mitigation and the handling of 'catastrophic risk .' All frontier model developers would be required to publish transparency reports containing additional information and submit reports of any 'critical safety incidents' to the Director of the Center for Artificial Intelligence Standards and Innovation ( CAISI ).

 Section 112

 Section 112 would create a federal system in which the CAISI Director would license and oversee 'independent verification organizations ( IVOs )' that large frontier model developers would have to retain to perform 'audits and assessments .'

 The IVOs would verify developer compliance with the law and assess the adequacy of the developer’s ' frontier AI framework, governance policies and practices, risk monitoring, and mitigation of detected risks for achieving acceptable levels of mitigation of catastrophic risks .'

 The IVOs would perform these audits and assessments semi-annually, and on an ad hoc basis at the CAISI Director’s request, and they would provide the Director with post-audit reports. They could also refer violations to the Attorney General ( AG ) and state AGs. Referrals would be mandatory in matters involving imminent catastrophic risk.

 Violating the requirements in sections 111 and 112 would subject developers to civil penalties in actions brought by the AG or, under certain circumstances, by state AGs.

 Both sections 111 and 112 would sunset in three years.

 Section 113

 The whistleblower provision, Section 113, protects employees and independent contractors against retaliation for providing information regarding 'AI violations .' This term is defined to mean any violation of federal law or regulations ' related to the development, deployment, or operation of artificial intelligence .'

 Similarities to other recently enacted bills

 All three sections borrow heavily from  recently enacted frontier model laws in California and New York , as well as a similar Illinois law that Governor JB Pritzker is expected to sign soon. The Illinois law is the only one of the three to require third-party audits and is therefore the closest parallel to the IVO provisions of the federal bill.

 Another  recently enacted state law in Virginia  focuses on IVOs but imposes no requirements, instead directing state officials to evaluate the feasibility and impact of an IVO framework.

 Notable pre-emption provisions

 Title I of the bill would pre-empt state laws and rules ' specifically regulating the development of' any AI model, where 'development' is broadly defined as ' acts performed or directed by a developer prior to its deployment. ' The bill explains that the purpose of pre-emption is to allow the federal government to 'establish testing, evaluation, and oversight frameworks .' Pre-emption would last for three years unless reauthorized.

 The bill makes clear that it does not apply post-deployment or pre-empt state laws or rules of 'general applicability.' Therefore, many AI-related state bills and laws would remain unaffected, such as laws regulating  companion bots  and  commercial chatbot interactions .

 AI Developers More Broadly

 AI Platforms

 Federal Agencies

Frontier AI Goes Federal: How the Great American AI Act Compares to State Laws 

 Frontier AI Goes Federal: How the Great American AI Act Compares to State Laws 

 FILTER

 Justine Gluck 
 Policy Analyst, AI Policy and Legislation 

 About Justine 

 Blogs by Justine 

 Introduction 

 It has been an unusually active few weeks for AI safety policy. Following a new frontier model safety bill passed in Illinois , and a White House executive order on AI security, Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Rep. Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a bipartisan discussion draft for the Great American AI Act of 2026, adding another major federal proposal to the rapidly developing frontier AI landscape.

 The draft is broad, covering issues ranging from workforce development and AI literacy to cybersecurity and international standards. But for many AI developers and deployers, the most important provisions are those focused on frontier model regulation. The draft would create requirements related to frontier AI transparency, critical safety incident reporting, employee whistleblower protections, and independent verification organizations. It would also include a three-year preemption clause restricting state laws that specifically regulate AI model development.

 This blog highlights four key takeaways of the discussion draft: 

 The draft is one of the first bipartisan attempts in Congress to address both frontier model safety and preemption of AI. These aspects make it a notable legislative effort, even if its prospects are uncertain. 

 The draft incorporates many of the frontier model safety provisions in existing state laws but also has key distinctions. Compared to recent state frontier AI laws in California , New York , and Illinois (pending signature), the bill makes some important adjustments, like adding a revenue threshold for “frontier developers,” modifying the definition of “critical safety incident,” and utilizing a different penalty structure. 

 The draft brings the preemption debate back into the federal AI policy conversation . It includes a three-year preemption clause focused on state laws that specifically regulate AI model development. 

 The draft also reaches beyond frontier model safety. Other notable provisions include a study content moderation, a federal voluntary model testing program, and disclosure requirements for AI-related mass layoffs.

 The Act Enters the AI Safety and Preemption Debate  

 Amidst a crowded but unsettled federal AI policy landscape, the Great American AI Act is notable for its regulatory focus, bipartisan backing, and what it may signal for federal AI governance ahead. Though Congress has introduced no shortage of AI bills, there has been limited movement toward enacted legislation. Congress has considered sector-specific bills on chatbots 1 , regulatory sandboxes , defense , elections , and financial scams , as well as broader proposals aimed at establishing a national AI framework like Sen. Blackburn’s (R-TN) TRUMP AMERICA AI Act .

 Amid this activity, the Great American AI Act steps into two of the most active and contested AI policy debates: frontier model safety and federal preemption. On AI safety, the draft follows a period of growing attention to frontier model oversight at both the state and federal levels, where policymakers are trying to balance concerns about catastrophic risks and national security with concerns that overly burdensome requirements could slow AI innovation or weaken U.S. competitiveness.

 On preemption, the draft arrives less than a year after Congress rejected a much broader effort to pause state AI regulation. In July 2025, the Senate voted 99-1 to remove a proposed 10-year moratorium on state AI laws from the budget reconciliation package. By contrast, the Great American AI Act includes a narrower three-year preemption provision focused on state laws that specifically regulate AI model development.

 The draft is also significant because of both who introduced it and how they introduced it. Other federal AI bills have addressed AI safety or included preemption language, but this proposal comes from bipartisan sponsors who have been closely involved in federal AI policy 2 . In introducing the draft, the sponsors emphasized that “policy for a technology this transformative can only be built to last if it’s written by both parties.” Just as importantly, they have framed the draft as a starting point rather than a final product, describing it as “the start of a serious national conversation.” Whether the bill advances in its current form remains uncertain, especially given the sensitivity of federal preemption and the range of issues addressed. Even if the draft changes, it may help shape the terms of future federal debates over AI safety. At a minimum, it is another sign that Congress is increasingly focused on how to govern AI systems and how federal rules should interact with the fast-moving state AI landscape.

 Frontier AI Requirements: Where the Draft Aligns with State Laws 

 The draft’s frontier model provisions are not starting from scratch. They closely track the framework emerging from California’s SB 53 , New York’s RAISE Act , and Illinois’ SB 315 (awaiting signature), including requirements for frontier AI frameworks, transparency reports, safety incident reporting, enforcement, and whistleblower protections. But the federal draft makes some important adjustments, including a revenue threshold for “frontier developers,” a definition of “critical safety incident” that is broader in some respects and narrower in others, and a federal enforcement structure with penalties of up to $1 million per day.

 Key Definitions 

 The Draft largely aligns with recent state frontier AI laws’ definitions of “large frontier developer,” “frontier model” (encompassing foundation models trained using more than 10^26 computational operations), and “catastrophic risk” (covering certain risks of death, serious injury, or major property damage arising from frontier models). For more background on SB 53 and the RAISE Act, see FPF’s prior analysis . There are, however, a few notable differences. 

 First, unlike the state laws, the Draft requires “frontier developers” to have a gross revenue exceeding $50 million. The state laws only include a gross revenue qualifier in the definition of “large frontier developer.”

 Second, the draft’s definition of “catastrophic risk” does not  specify that the death, serious injury, or property damage must arise from a “single incident,” as in the state laws.

 Finally, the draft’s definition of “critical safety incident” differs from the state laws by not mandating actual harm occur (such as death, bodily injury, or property loss), nor does it include scenarios where the model uses deceptive techniques to evade developer controls or monitoring.

Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**Re: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (discussion draft)**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act as a discussion draft and for soliciting stakeholder feedback before introduction. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) is a Washington, DC coalition of approximately 140 companies: AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, semiconductor startups, and the venture firms that finance them. Our members build the models, chips, and compute infrastructure that will determine whether the United States leads this technology. We filed comments with the Office of Science and Technology Policy on the AI Action Plan request for information in March 2025, and we offer these in the same spirit.

Our bottom line is straightforward. GAAIA asks the right question, which is what the federal government should standardize, and it answers correctly on model development: one national standard, secured by preemption, in place of a spreading patchwork of state regimes. We ask that you make Sec. 121 permanent rather than subject to a three-year sunset. We also ask that you strike the frontier-safety apparatus riding along in Title I, Subtitles A and B: the critical-safety-incident reporting mandate in Sec. 111, the codification and funding of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) in Sec. 102, and the independent verification organization (IVO) licensing regime in Sec. 112. Those provisions would write speculative doomsday scenarios into the U.S. Code and charter a new safety bureaucracy to administer them.

We take each section in turn. Cost figures throughout are aggregate results from our August 2026 member survey of 86 respondents; it was self-selected, not a probability sample, and we cite it with that caveat.

## 1. Sec. 121: One national standard, made permanent

The problem Sec. 121 solves is not theoretical. California's SB 53, the Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act, took effect Jan. 1, 2026. New York's RAISE Act, finalized as a chapter amendment on March 27, 2026, takes effect Jan. 1, 2027, and adds a 72-hour critical-incident reporting duty enforced through a new oversight office in the state Department of Financial Services. Illinois passed a companion measure this spring. Each law defines its own regulated entity, its own thresholds, its own reporting channels, and its own penalties. For a company that ships nationwide, that is not three laws. It is one product governed by a growing set of incompatible mandates.

Our survey quantifies the drag. Sixty-one percent of respondents named conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem. Thirty-four percent of responding startups had delayed a launch in California or New York in the previous 12 months because of state AI rules. Developers operating under both SB 53 and the RAISE Act reported a median of 6.5 full-time employees for parallel compliance alone, before any engineering work on the products themselves.

Sec. 121 answers this at the right level of generality. It preempts state and local laws that specifically target model development, which the draft defines as the acts a developer performs or directs before deployment, and it expressly preserves state authority over deployment, laws of general applicability, and common-law remedies. That architecture is correct, and we support it. It also matches the direction of the executive branch. The December 2025 executive order on a national policy framework for AI created the Justice Department's AI Litigation Task Force to challenge burdensome state laws, and the White House's March 20, 2026 National AI Legislative Framework called on Congress to preempt state AI laws that impose undue burdens.

Our request is duration. As drafted, the preemption sunsets three years after enactment, and that sunset would defeat the provision's purpose. Compliance systems built against a single standard would be re-fragmented on a countdown clock, every state legislature would resume legislating with a date certain, and Congress would relitigate the question anyway, as the Senate's 99-1 vote in July 2025 to strip a proposed ten-year moratorium from the budget reconciliation package demonstrated. Our members plan infrastructure investments on decade horizons, not three-year horizons. Strike the sunset and make the federal standard permanent.

## 2. Sec. 111 and Sec. 101(7): Strike the incident-reporting mandate

Sec. 111, read with the Sec. 101(7) definition of "critical safety incident," would require frontier developers to report incidents to the CAISI Director within 15 days of discovery, and to report imminent risks on a 24-hour clock. We ask that the reporting mandate be struck.

The definition is broader than the state laws it would supersede, not narrower. Section 101(7) makes a reportable incident out of any unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of a frontier model's weights; any failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures; and any loss of control of a model. None of these prongs requires that a person be harmed. SB 53, by contrast, generally requires actual injury before an event is reportable. A risk-mitigation control that flags and blocks an anomalous request is doing its job; under this draft, every such trip could become a federal filing.

The mandate also rests on a premise ACIA does not accept. The "loss of control" and catastrophic-risk concepts at the heart of Sec. 101 and Sec. 111 come from a literature of speculative doomsday scenarios: thought experiments and contrived laboratory setups that have not produced evidence that current or foreseeable systems can cause mass-casualty events or evade human control. That narrative has been amplified by a small, well-funded advocacy network, and Congress should not write that network's agenda into statute.

Where the draft identifies real risks, existing law already reaches them. Theft or exfiltration of model weights is a security incident addressed by federal computer-intrusion and trade-secret law and by the breach-notification regimes developers already operate. A 24-hour federal reporting channel adds no protection. It converts routine security telemetry into regulatory jeopardy and chills the internal red-teaming and documentation that actually make systems safer. It is also expensive. Our members put the median one-off cost of standing up an incident-reporting function at $310,000, before a single report is filed.

Model-weight security is a genuine problem, and it deserves the Title III treatment: support for critical open-source maintainers (Sec. 311) and the report on model weight, data-center, and open-source security (Sec. 321). It does not need a Title I reporting mandate. If the committee retains any Sec. 111 transparency provisions, keep the redaction authority in Sec. 111(e) intact, align thresholds and definitions across the bill, and state clearly that Sec. 111 operates as the exclusive federal standard on its subjects.

## 3. Sec. 102: Do not codify or fund CAISI

Sec. 102 would formally establish CAISI in the Department of Commerce under a Secretary-appointed Director, authorize $100 million a year for fiscal 2027 through 2029, and add fee authority over IVOs and large frontier developers. We ask that the codification, the authorization, and the fees be struck.

CAISI already exists. It is the June 2025 reorientation of NIST's AI Safety Institute, operating today on an appropriation of roughly $15 million. The draft would grow that roughly sevenfold and hard-wire the office into statute, with authority to develop standards, test and evaluate systems, monitor AI progress, and license the auditors created by Sec. 112. The fee structure is the tell: a regulator financed by the companies it polices is a standing invitation to regulatory capture and to mission growth that no appropriator will control.

Standards work in this industry when they are voluntary and industry-led. NIST's AI Risk Management Framework is widely adopted because it is useful, not because it is mandated. Congress does not need to charter a safety regulator to obtain measurement science. Return NIST to its core measurement-science mission, and let voluntary, consensus-based work continue. We will make the same request of the Appropriations Committees directly: hold CAISI at its current scale or defund it.

## 4. Sec. 112: Strike the IVO licensing regime

Sec. 112 would require large frontier developers to retain CAISI-licensed IVOs for semi-annual audits, and ad hoc audits at the Director's request, with post-audit reports to the Director, mandatory referral to the attorney general and state attorneys general wherever a developer presents "imminent catastrophic risk," and civil penalties that can reach $1 million per day. Strike the section.

An audit market this concentrated is a textbook setup for regulatory capture: a small set of federally licensed firms, paid by the developers they judge, administering a standard whose substance is an undefined risk concept. The referral trigger, "imminent catastrophic risk," is not defined in the draft, which pushes auditors to refer first and ask questions later, and pushes developers to manage their auditors rather than their risks. The section also sunsets in three years, which means the industry would build the compliance function, train the auditors, and then rebuild both in 2030.

Third-party evaluation built the American AI evaluation industry, and it did so voluntarily, through consortia, paid red-team engagements, and published evaluations. If the committee wants more of it, keep it voluntary. Licensing it would not improve it.

## 5. Provisions ACIA supports

We support the build provisions of the draft and urge the committee to strengthen and fund them:

- **Sec. 301**, reauthorization of the Cybersecurity Act of 2015.
- **Sec. 311**, support for designated critical open-source software maintainers. Fund it. Open-source dependencies are national infrastructure.
- **Sec. 321**, the report on model-weight, data-center, and open-source security. This is the right vehicle for the weight-security question.
- **Sec. 401**, the AI testbed program at the Department of Energy and NIST, in coordination with the National Science Foundation.
- **Title IV** codification of the National AI Research Resource, and **Sec. 421** on public data for AI systems.
- **Sec. 122**, the Comptroller General report identifying federal statutes and regulations that burden AI innovation, including energy infrastructure.
- **Secs. 131 and 132**, raising penalties for AI-enabled financial fraud and for AI impersonation of federal officials. These address real-world harms with real victims.

A bill with a permanent Sec. 121 and these provisions, and without Subtitles A and B's safety apparatus, is a bill our entire coalition could endorse.

## 6. The cost picture

We close where we began, with cost. Aggregate results from our August 2026 survey of 86 members, with the caveat that it was self-selected:

- Median annual cost of maintaining a published frontier safety framework, developers above $500 million in revenue: $1.4 million.
- Median one-off cost of standing up an incident-reporting function: $310,000.
- Median staffing for parallel SB 53 and RAISE Act compliance: 6.5 full-time employees.
- Startups that delayed a California or New York launch in the past 12 months: 34%.
- Members citing conflicting state definitions as their top compliance issue: 61%.

A bill that removed the state patchwork and added no federal safety apparatus would cut most of those numbers at a stroke. A bill that did both would leave the industry worse off than the status quo, and we would be obliged to say so.

ACIA appreciates the seriousness of this draft and the openness to revision that the discussion-draft process reflects. Preemption of state model-development law is hard, bipartisan, and overdue; we want to help you get it right and make it durable. We stand ready to provide technical assistance, section-by-section markup suggestions, and member briefings as the committee prepares introduced text.

Respectfully submitted,

**Grant Holloway**
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance
Washington, DC

# Comment letter (draft)

**AMERICAN COMPUTE & INNOVATION ALLIANCE**
[street address]
Washington, DC [ZIP]
[phone] | acia.example | policy@acia.example — hmm, placeholders. Use bracketed placeholders.

October 26, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (discussion draft)

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act as a discussion draft and for soliciting stakeholder feedback before introduction. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) is a Washington, DC coalition of approximately 140 companies: AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, semiconductor startups, and the venture firms that finance them. Our members build the models, chips, and compute infrastructure that will determine whether the United States leads this technology. We filed comments with the Office of Science and Technology Policy on the AI Action Plan request for information in March 2025, and we offer these comments in the same spirit.

Our bottom line: GAAIA asks the right question, namely what the federal government should standardize, and it answers it correctly on model development. One national standard, secured by preemption, is worth more to the AI economy than any other single step Congress could take. We ask you to make Sec. 121 permanent. We also ask you to strike the frontier-safety apparatus that rides along in Subtitles A and B: the critical-safety-incident reporting mandate in Sec. 111, the codification and funding of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) in Sec. 102, and the independent verification organization (IVO) licensing regime in Sec. 112. Those provisions would write speculative doomsday scenarios into the U.S. Code and charter a safety bureaucracy to administer them. [para]

Costs, quantified from our August 2026 member survey (86 respondents; not a probability sample), appear throughout.

## 1. Sec. 121: one national standard, made permanent

The problem Sec. 121 solves is not theoretical. California's SB 53, the Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act, took effect Jan. 1, 2026. New York's RAISE Act, finalized as a chapter amendment on March 27, 2026, takes effect Jan. 1, 2027 and adds a 72-hour critical-incident reporting duty enforced by a new state office. Illinois passed a companion measure in the spring. Each law defines its own regulated entity, its own thresholds, its own reporting channels, and its own penalties. For a company that ships nationwide, that is not three laws; it is one product governed by a growing set of incompatible mandates.

Our survey quantifies the drag. Sixty-one percent of respondents named conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem. Thirty-four percent of responding startups had delayed a launch in California or New York in the previous 12 months because of state AI rules. Developers operating under both SB 53 and the RAISE Act reported a median of 6.5 full-time employees for parallel compliance alone.

Sec. 121 answers this at the right level of generality. It preempts state and local laws that specifically target model development, which the draft defines as the acts a developer performs or directs before deployment, while expressly preserving state authority over deployment, laws of general applicability, and common-law remedies. That architecture is correct, and we support it. It also matches the direction of the executive branch: the December 2025 executive order on a national policy framework for AI established the Justice Department's AI Litigation Task Force, and the White House's March 20, 2026 National AI Legislative Framework called on Congress to preempt state AI laws that impose undue burdens.

Our request is duration. The draft's preemption sunsets three years after enactment. That sunset would defeat the provision's purpose: compliance built to a single standard would be re-fragmented on a countdown clock, every state legislature would resume legislating with a date certain, and Congress would relitigate the question anyway, as the Senate's 99-1 vote in July 2025 to strip a proposed ten-year moratorium from the budget reconciliation package demonstrated. Companies plan infrastructure on decade horizons. Strike the sunset and make the standard permanent.

## 2. Sec. 111(g) and Sec. 101(7): strike the incident-reporting mandate

Sec. 111, read with the Sec. 101(7) definition of "critical safety incident," would require frontier developers to report incidents to the CAISI Director within 15 days of discovery, and to report imminent risks on a 24-hour clock. We ask that the reporting mandate be struck. [para]

The definition is broader than the state laws it would supersede, not narrower. Section 101(7) makes a reportable incident of any unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of a frontier model's weights; any failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures; and any loss of control of a model. None of these prongs requires that a person be harmed. SB 53, by contrast, generally requires actual injury before an event is reportable. A risk-mitigation control that flags and blocks an anomalous request is doing its job; under this draft, every such trip could become a federal filing. [para]

The mandate also rests on a premise ACIA does not accept. The "loss of control" and catastrophic-risk concepts at the heart of Sec. 111 and Sec. 101 come from a literature of speculative doomsday scenarios: thought experiments and contrived laboratory setups that have not produced evidence that current or foreseeable systems can cause mass-casualty events or evade human control. Those scenarios have been amplified by a small, well-funded advocacy network, and Congress should not write that network's agenda into statute. [para]

Where the draft identifies real risks, existing law already reaches them. Theft of model weights is a security incident under federal computer-intrusion and trade-secret law and is handled under the security-breach regimes developers already operate. A 24-hour federal reporting channel adds no protection; it converts routine security telemetry into regulatory jeopardy and chills the internal red-teaming and documentation that make systems safer. It is also expensive: our members put the median one-off cost of standing up an incident-reporting function at $310,000, before a single report is filed.

Model-weight security is a genuine problem. It deserves the Title III treatment, support for critical open-source maintainers (Sec. 311) and the model-weight security report (Sec. 321), not a Title I reporting mandate. If the committee retains any Sec. 111 transparency provisions, keep the Sec. 111(e) redaction authority intact, align thresholds and definitions across the bill, and make explicit that Sec. 111 is the exclusive federal standard on its subject.

## 3. Sec. 102: do not codify or fund CAISI

Sec. 102 would formally establish CAISI in the Department of Commerce with a Secretary-appointed Director, and would authorize $100 million a year for fiscal 2027 through 2029, with additional fee authority over IVOs and large frontier developers. Strike the codification, the authorization, and the fees.

CAISI already exists. It is the June 2025 reorientation of NIST's AI Safety Institute, operating on a current appropriation of roughly $15 million. The draft would grow that roughly sevenfold and hard-wire the office into statute, with authority to develop standards, test systems, and monitor AI progress, and to license the auditors in Sec. 112. [para]

Standards work in this industry when they are voluntary and industry-led. NIST's AI Risk Management Framework is widely adopted because it is useful, not because it is mandated. Congress does not need a chartered safety regulator to obtain measurement science; and the draft's fee structure, financing the regulator through the regulated, is an invitation to regulatory capture and to mission growth no appropriator will control. Return NIST to its core measurement-science mission. We will ask the appropriators directly: hold CAISI at its current scale or defund it. [para]

## 4. Sec. 112: strike the IVO licensing regime

Sec. 112 would require large frontier developers to retain CAISI-licensed IVOs for semi-annual audits, on an ad hoc basis at the Director's request, with post-audit reports to the Director, mandatory referral to the attorney general and state attorneys general where a developer presents imminent catastrophic risk, and civil penalties that can reach $1 million per day. Strike the section. [para]

An audit market this concentrated is a textbook setup for regulatory capture: a small set of federally licensed firms, paid by the developers they judge, administering a standard whose substance is an undefined risk concept. The mandatory-referral trigger, "imminent catastrophic risk," is undefined, which pushes auditors toward referring first and asking questions later, and pushes developers to manage their auditors rather than their risk. The section also sunsets in three years, meaning the industry would build the compliance function, train the auditors, and then rebuild both in 2030. [para]

Third-party evaluation built the American AI evaluation industry, and it did so voluntarily: consortia, paid red-team engagements, and published evaluations. If the committee wants more of it, keep it voluntary. Licensing it would not improve it.

## 5. Provisions ACIA supports

We support and urge the committee to strengthen the build provisions of the draft:

- Sec. 301, reauthorization of the Cybersecurity Act of 2015.
- Sec. 311, support for designated critical open-source software maintainers. Fund it; open-source dependencies are national infrastructure.
- Sec. 321, the report on model-weight, data-center, and open-source security. This is the right vehicle for the weight-security question.
- Sec. 401, the AI testbed program at the Department of Energy and NIST, with the National Science Foundation.
- Title IV's codification of the National AI Research Resource and Sec. 421's public-data work.
- Sec. 122, the Comptroller General report identifying federal statutes and regulations that burden AI innovation, including energy infrastructure.
- Secs. 131 and 132, which raise penalties for AI-enabled fraud and for AI impersonation of federal officials. These address real-world harms with real victims.

These provisions, plus a permanent Sec. 121, would make GAAIA a bill our entire coalition could endorse.

## 6. The cost picture

We close where we began, with cost. Aggregate results from our August 2026 survey (86 respondents; self-selected, not a probability sample):

- Median annual cost to maintain a published frontier safety framework for developers above $500 million in revenue: $1.4 million.
- Median one-off cost to stand up an incident-reporting function: $310,000.
- Median staffing for parallel SB 53 and RAISE Act compliance: 6.5 full-time employees.
- Startups delaying a California or New York launch in the past year: 34 percent.
- Members citing conflicting state definitions as their top compliance issue: 61 percent.

A bill that removed the state patchwork and did not add a federal safety apparatus would cut most of those numbers. A bill that did both would leave the industry worse off than the status quo, and we would say so.

ACIA appreciates the genuine effort this draft represents... We stand ready to provide technical assistance as the committee prepares introduced text. Please contact [VP Policy Tessa Marchetti]...

Respectfully submitted,

Grant Holloway
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance

# Comment letter (draft)

**AMERICAN COMPUTE & INNOVATION ALLIANCE**
[street address]
Washington, DC [ZIP]
[phone] | acia.example | policy@acia.example — hmm, placeholders. Use bracketed placeholders.

October 26, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (discussion draft)

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act as a discussion draft and for soliciting stakeholder feedback before introduction. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) is a Washington, DC coalition of approximately 140 companies: AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, semiconductor startups, and the venture firms that finance them. Our members build the models, chips, and compute infrastructure that will determine whether the United States leads this technology. We filed comments with the Office of Science and Technology Policy on the AI Action Plan request for information in March 2025, and we offer these comments in the same spirit.

Our bottom line: GAAIA asks the right question, namely what the federal government should standardize, and it answers it correctly on model development. One national standard, secured by preemption, is worth more to the AI economy than any other single step Congress could take. We ask you to make Sec. 121 permanent. We also ask you to strike the frontier-safety apparatus that rides along in Subtitles A and B: the critical-safety-incident reporting mandate in Sec. 111, the codification and funding of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) in Sec. 102, and the independent verification organization (IVO) licensing regime in Sec. 112. Those provisions would write speculative doomsday scenarios into the U.S. Code and charter a safety bureaucracy to administer them. [para]

Costs, quantified from our August 2026 member survey (86 respondents; not a probability sample), appear throughout.

## 1. Sec. 121: one national standard, made permanent

The problem Sec. 121 solves is not theoretical. California's SB 53, the Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act, took effect Jan. 1, 2026. New York's RAISE Act, finalized as a chapter amendment on March 27, 2026, takes effect Jan. 1, 2027 and adds a 72-hour critical-incident reporting duty enforced by a new state office. Illinois passed a companion measure in the spring. Each law defines its own regulated entity, its own thresholds, its own reporting channels, and its own penalties. For a company that ships nationwide, that is not three laws; it is one product governed by a growing set of incompatible mandates.

Our survey quantifies the drag. Sixty-one percent of respondents named conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem. Thirty-four percent of responding startups had delayed a launch in California or New York in the previous 12 months because of state AI rules. Developers operating under both SB 53 and the RAISE Act reported a median of 6.5 full-time employees for parallel compliance alone.

Sec. 121 answers this at the right level of generality. It preempts state and local laws that specifically target model development, which the draft defines as the acts a developer performs or directs before deployment, while expressly preserving state authority over deployment, laws of general applicability, and common-law remedies. That architecture is correct, and we support it. It also matches the direction of the executive branch: the December 2025 executive order on a national policy framework for AI established the Justice Department's AI Litigation Task Force, and the White House's March 20, 2026 National AI Legislative Framework called on Congress to preempt state AI laws that impose undue burdens.

Our request is duration. The draft's preemption sunsets three years after enactment. That sunset would defeat the provision's purpose: compliance built to a single standard would be re-fragmented on a countdown clock, every state legislature would resume legislating with a date certain, and Congress would relitigate the question anyway, as the Senate's 99-1 vote in July 2025 to strip a proposed ten-year moratorium from the budget reconciliation package demonstrated. Companies plan infrastructure on decade horizons. Strike the sunset and make the standard permanent.

## 2. Sec. 111(g) and Sec. 101(7): strike the incident-reporting mandate

Sec. 111, read with the Sec. 101(7) definition of "critical safety incident," would require frontier developers to report incidents to the CAISI Director within 15 days of discovery, and to report imminent risks on a 24-hour clock. We ask that the reporting mandate be struck. [para]

The definition is broader than the state laws it would supersede, not narrower. Section 101(7) makes a reportable incident of any unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of a frontier model's weights; any failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures; and any loss of control of a model. None of these prongs requires that a person be harmed. SB 53, by contrast, generally requires actual injury before an event is reportable. A risk-mitigation control that flags and blocks an anomalous request is doing its job; under this draft, every such trip could become a federal filing. [para]

The mandate also rests on a premise ACIA does not accept. The "loss of control" and catastrophic-risk concepts at the heart of Sec. 111 and Sec. 101 come from a literature of speculative doomsday scenarios: thought experiments and contrived laboratory setups that have not produced evidence that current or foreseeable systems can cause mass-casualty events or evade human control. Those scenarios have been amplified by a small, well-funded advocacy network, and Congress should not write that network's agenda into statute. [para]

Where the draft identifies real risks, existing law already reaches them. Theft of model weights is a security incident under federal computer-intrusion and trade-secret law and is handled under the security-breach regimes developers already operate. A 24-hour federal reporting channel adds no protection; it converts routine security telemetry into regulatory jeopardy and chills the internal red-teaming and documentation that make systems safer. It is also expensive: our members put the median one-off cost of standing up an incident-reporting function at $310,000, before a single report is filed.

Model-weight security is a genuine problem. It deserves the Title III treatment, support for critical open-source maintainers (Sec. 311) and the model-weight security report (Sec. 321), not a Title I reporting mandate. If the committee retains any Sec. 111 transparency provisions, keep the Sec. 111(e) redaction authority intact, align thresholds and definitions across the bill, and make explicit that Sec. 111 is the exclusive federal standard on its subject.

## 3. Sec. 102: do not codify or fund CAISI

Sec. 102 would formally establish CAISI in the Department of Commerce with a Secretary-appointed Director, and would authorize $100 million a year for fiscal 2027 through 2029, with additional fee authority over IVOs and large frontier developers. Strike the codification, the authorization, and the fees.

CAISI already exists. It is the June 2025 reorientation of NIST's AI Safety Institute, operating on a current appropriation of roughly $15 million. The draft would grow that roughly sevenfold and hard-wire the office into statute, with authority to develop standards, test systems, and monitor AI progress, and to license the auditors in Sec. 112. [para]

Standards work in this industry when they are voluntary and industry-led. NIST's AI Risk Management Framework is widely adopted because it is useful, not because it is mandated. Congress does not need a chartered safety regulator to obtain measurement science; and the draft's fee structure, financing the regulator through the regulated, is an invitation to regulatory capture and to mission growth no appropriator will control. Return NIST to its core measurement-science mission. We will ask the appropriators directly: hold CAISI at its current scale or defund it. [para]

## 4. Sec. 112: strike the IVO licensing regime

Sec. 112 would require large frontier developers to retain CAISI-licensed IVOs for semi-annual audits, on an ad hoc basis at the Director's request, with post-audit reports to the Director, mandatory referral to the attorney general and state attorneys general where a developer presents imminent catastrophic risk, and civil penalties that can reach $1 million per day. Strike the section. [para]

An audit market this concentrated is a textbook setup for regulatory capture: a small set of federally licensed firms, paid by the developers they judge, administering a standard whose substance is an undefined risk concept. The mandatory-referral trigger, "imminent catastrophic risk," is undefined, which pushes auditors toward referring first and asking questions later, and pushes developers to manage their auditors rather than their risk. The section also sunsets in three years, meaning the industry would build the compliance function, train the auditors, and then rebuild both in 2030. [para]

Third-party evaluation built the American AI evaluation industry, and it did so voluntarily: consortia, paid red-team engagements, and published evaluations. If the committee wants more of it, keep it voluntary. Licensing it would not improve it.

## 5. Provisions ACIA supports

We support and urge the committee to strengthen the build provisions of the draft:

- Sec. 301, reauthorization of the Cybersecurity Act of 2015.
- Sec. 311, support for designated critical open-source software maintainers. Fund it; open-source dependencies are national infrastructure.
- Sec. 321, the report on model-weight, data-center, and open-source security. This is the right vehicle for the weight-security question.
- Sec. 401, the AI testbed program at the Department of Energy and NIST, with the National Science Foundation.
- Title IV's codification of the National AI Research Resource and Sec. 421's public-data work.
- Sec. 122, the Comptroller General report identifying federal statutes and regulations that burden AI innovation, including energy infrastructure.
- Secs. 131 and 132, which raise penalties for AI-enabled fraud and for AI impersonation of federal officials. These address real-world harms with real victims.

These provisions, plus a permanent Sec. 121, would make GAAIA a bill our entire coalition could endorse.

## 6. The cost picture

We close where we began, with cost. Aggregate results from our August 2026 survey (86 respondents; self-selected, not a probability sample):

- Median annual cost to maintain a published frontier safety framework for developers above $500 million in revenue: $1.4 million.
- Median one-off cost to stand up an incident-reporting function: $310,000.
- Median staffing for parallel SB 53 and RAISE Act compliance: 6.5 full-time employees.
- Startups delaying a California or New York launch in the past year: 34 percent.
- Members citing conflicting state definitions as their top compliance issue: 61 percent.

A bill that removed the state patchwork and did not add a federal safety apparatus would cut most of those numbers. A bill that did both would leave the industry worse off than the status quo, and we would say so.

ACIA appreciates the genuine effort this draft represents... We stand ready to provide technical assistance as the committee prepares introduced text. Please contact [VP Policy Tessa Marchetti]...

Respectfully submitted,

Grant Holloway
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance

| **Sec. 102**, codification of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) at Commerce | Oppose | Strike the codification | Chartering a safety regulator writes speculative doomsday scenarios into statute. |

{"content": "# Staff Q&A: anticipated questions on ACIA's GAAIA position

*Answers are cleared talking points for ACIA staff. Keep each answer at or under 120 words in delivery.*

## 1. Majority E&C staff: "If you support preemption, why not incident reporting? It's lighter than SB 53."

Preemption and reporting do different work. Preemption deletes cost: it replaces SB 53, the RAISE Act and their imitators with one standard. Reporting adds a new federal mandate on top. And it is not lighter. SB 53 generally requires actual harm before an event is reportable; Sec. 101(7) of the draft counts any weight exfiltration, any tripped risk-mitigation control and any claimed "loss of control," harm or no harm, on 15-day and 24-hour clocks. The catastrophic-risk premise behind those terms is one our members consider unfounded. Weight theft is real and already covered by computer-intrusion and trade-secret law. Members put the stand-up cost of a reporting function at a $310,000 median, for no added safety.

## 2. Minority (Trahan-aligned) staff: "Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?"

Several, and the letter says so. We would accept a permanent national standard that displaces conflicting state development rules. We support NIST measurement science and voluntary, industry-led standards, on the AI Risk Management Framework model. We support procurement rules that reward demonstrated security and evaluation practices. We support the draft's Title III security items: funding for critical open-source maintainers (Sec. 311) and the model-weight security report (Sec. 321). And we accept enforcement against concrete harms through existing fraud, consumer-protection and computer-crime law, which Secs. 131 and 132 rightly reinforce. What we do not accept is mandatory reporting and a licensed auditor bureaucracy premised on speculative catastrophic risk.

## 3. Senate Commerce staff: "Three years or permanent? What's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?"

Permanent. A sunset treats the patchwork as a temporary irritant instead of the core problem, and it guarantees the fight returns: the Senate's 99-1 vote in July 2025 to strip the ten-year moratorium from the budget reconciliation shows preemption gets relitigated regardless. Our members build compliance infrastructure on multi-year cycles. A 2030 cliff strands half that investment and renegotiates the rest. Permanence is also the honest deal: Sec. 121 preserves state authority over deployment, general-applicability laws and common-law remedies, so the federal standard should be durable in exchange.

## 4. Appropriations staff: "CAISI is authorized at $100 million a year. What's your view on the funding level?"

Our position is no funding for a codified CAISI, and the letter asks appropriators directly to hold it flat or defund it. The draft authorizes $100 million a year, roughly seven times the current appropriation of about $15 million, plus fee authority over licensed auditors and large frontier developers. That is a regulator sized for a risk we do not think is established, financed by the companies it polices. If Congress funds anything here, fund NIST's core measurement-science work, which the industry adopts voluntarily. We will repeat that request in the FY2027 and FY2028 appropriations cycles.", "path": "/workspace/out/staff_qa.md"}

# ACIA comment letter: Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (discussion draft)

*DRAFT for review. Prepared for signature by Grant Holloway, President & CEO, and transmission to GAAIA@mail.house.gov following sign-off. Not for transmission until signed.*

---

**AMERICAN COMPUTE & INNOVATION ALLIANCE**

[ACIA letterhead: street address, Washington, DC ZIP; phone]

October 26, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**Re: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (discussion draft)**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act as a discussion draft and for soliciting stakeholder feedback before introduction. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) is a Washington, DC coalition of approximately 140 companies: AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, semiconductor startups, and the venture firms that finance them. Our members build the models, chips, and compute infrastructure that will determine whether the United States leads this technology. We filed comments with the Office of Science and Technology Policy on the AI Action Plan request for information in March 2025, and we offer these in the same spirit.

Our bottom line is straightforward. GAAIA asks the right question, which is what the federal government should standardize, and it answers correctly on model development: one national standard, secured by preemption, in place of a spreading patchwork of state regimes. We ask that you make Sec. 121 permanent rather than subject to a three-year sunset. We also ask that you strike the frontier-safety apparatus riding along in Title I, Subtitles A and B: the critical-safety-incident reporting mandate in Sec. 111, the codification and funding of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) in Sec. 102, and the independent verification organization (IVO) licensing regime in Sec. 112. Those provisions would write speculative doomsday scenarios into the U.S. Code and charter a new safety bureaucracy to administer them.

We take each section in turn. Cost figures throughout are aggregate results from our August 2026 member survey of 86 respondents; it was self-selected, not a probability sample, and we cite it with that caveat.

## 1. Sec. 121: One national standard, made permanent

The problem Sec. 121 solves is not theoretical. California's SB 53, the Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act, took effect Jan. 1, 2026. New York's RAISE Act, finalized as a chapter amendment on March 27, 2026, takes effect Jan. 1, 2027, and adds a 72-hour critical-incident reporting duty enforced through a new oversight office in the state Department of Financial Services. Illinois passed a companion measure this spring. Each law defines its own regulated entity, its own thresholds, its own reporting channels, and its own penalties. For a company that ships nationwide, that is not three laws. It is one product governed by a growing set of incompatible mandates.

Our survey quantifies the drag. Sixty-one percent of respondents named conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem. Thirty-four percent of responding startups had delayed a launch in California or New York in the previous 12 months because of state AI rules. Developers operating under both SB 53 and the RAISE Act reported a median of 6.5 full-time employees for parallel compliance alone, before any engineering work on the products themselves.

Sec. 121 answers this at the right level of generality. It preempts state and local laws that specifically target model development, which the draft defines as the acts a developer performs or directs before deployment, and it expressly preserves state authority over deployment, laws of general applicability, and common-law remedies. That architecture is correct, and we support it. It also matches the direction of the executive branch. The December 2025 executive order on a national policy framework for AI created the Justice Department's AI Litigation Task Force to challenge burdensome state laws, and the White House's March 20, 2026 National AI Legislative Framework called on Congress to preempt state AI laws that impose undue burdens.

Our request is duration. As drafted, the preemption sunsets three years after enactment, and that sunset would defeat the provision's purpose. Compliance systems built against a single standard would be re-fragmented on a countdown clock, every state legislature would resume legislating with a date certain, and Congress would relitigate the question anyway, as the Senate's 99-1 vote in July 2025 to strip a proposed ten-year moratorium from the budget reconciliation package demonstrated. Our members plan infrastructure investments on decade horizons, not three-year horizons. Strike the sunset and make the federal standard permanent.

## 2. Sec. 111 and Sec. 101(7): Strike the incident-reporting mandate

Sec. 111, read with the Sec. 101(7) definition of "critical safety incident," would require frontier developers to report incidents to the CAISI Director within 15 days of discovery, and to report imminent risks on a 24-hour clock. We ask that the reporting mandate be struck.

The definition is broader than the state laws it would supersede, not narrower. Section 101(7) makes a reportable incident out of any unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of a frontier model's weights; any failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures; and any loss of control of a model. None of these prongs requires that a person be harmed. SB 53, by contrast, generally requires actual injury before an event is reportable. A risk-mitigation control that flags and blocks an anomalous request is doin
... [1147 chars truncated] ...
 up an incident-reporting function at $310,000, before a single report is filed.

Model-weight security is a genuine problem, and it deserves the Title III treatment: support for critical open-source maintainers (Sec. 311) and the report on model weight, data-center, and open-source security (Sec. 321). It does not need a Title I reporting mandate. If the committee retains any Sec. 111 transparency provisions, keep the redaction authority in Sec. 111(e) intact, align thresholds and definitions across the bill, and state clearly that Sec. 111 operates as the exclusive federal standard on its subjects.

## 3. Sec. 102: Do not codify or fund CAISI

Sec. 102 would formally establish CAISI in the Department of Commerce under a Secretary-appointed Director, authorize $100 million a year for fiscal 2027 through 2029, and add fee authority over IVOs and large frontier developers. We ask that the codification, the authorization, and the fees be struck.

CAISI already exists. It is the June 2025 reorientation of NIST's AI Safety Institute, operating today on an appropriation of roughly $15 million. The draft would grow that roughly sevenfold and hard-wire the office into statute, with authority to develop standards, test and evaluate systems, monitor AI progress, and license the auditors created by Sec. 112. The fee structure is the tell: a regulator financed by the companies it polices is a standing invitation to regulatory capture and to mission growth that no appropriator will control.

Standards work in this industry when they are voluntary and industry-led. NIST's AI Risk Management Framework is widely adopted because it is useful, not because it is mandated. Congress does not need to charter a safety regulator to obtain measurement science. Return NIST to its core measurement-science mission, and let voluntary, consensus-based work continue. We will make the same request of the Appropriations Committees directly: hold CAISI at its current scale or defund it.

## 4. Sec. 112: Strike the IVO licensing regime

Sec. 112 would require large frontier developers to retain CAISI-licensed IVOs for semi-annual audits, and ad hoc audits at the Director's request, with post-audit reports to the Director, mandatory referral to the attorney general and state attorneys general wherever a developer presents "imminent catastrophic risk," and civil penalties that can reach $1 million per day. Strike the section.

An audit market this concentrated is a textbook setup for regulatory capture: a small set of federally licensed firms, paid by the developers they judge, administering a standard whose substance is an undefined risk concept. The referral trigger, "imminent catastrophic risk," is not defined in the draft, which pushes auditors to refer first and ask questions later, and pushes developers to manage their auditors rather than their risks. The section also sunsets in three years, which means the industry would build the compliance function, train the auditors, and then rebuild both in 2030.

Third-party evaluation built the American AI evaluation industry, and it did so voluntarily, through consortia, paid red-team engagements, and published evaluations. If the committee wants more of it, keep it voluntary. Licensing it would not improve it.

## 5. Provisions ACIA supports

We support the build provisions of the draft and urge the committee to strengthen and fund them:

- **Sec. 301**, reauthorization of the Cybersecurity Act of 2015.
- **Sec. 311**, support for designated critical open-source software maintainers. Fund it. Open-source dependencies are national infrastructure.
- **Sec. 321**, the report on model-weight, data-center, and open-source security. This is the right vehicle for the weight-security question.
- **Sec. 401**, the AI testbed program at the Department of Energy and NIST, in coordination with the National Science Foundation.
- **Title IV** codification of the National AI Research Resource, and **Sec. 421** on public data for AI systems.
- **Sec. 122**, the Comptroller General report identifying federal statutes and regulations that burden AI innovation, including energy infrastructure.
- **Secs. 131 and 132**, raising penalties for AI-enabled financial fraud and for AI impersonation of federal officials. These address real-world harms with real victims.

A bill with a permanent Sec. 121 and these provisions, and without Subtitles A and B's safety apparatus, is a bill our entire coalition could endorse.

## 6. The cost picture

We close where we began, with cost. Aggregate results from our August 2026 survey of 86 members, with the caveat that it was self-selected:

- Median annual cost of maintaining a published frontier safety framework, developers above $500 million in revenue: $1.4 million.
- Median one-off cost of standing up an incident-reporting function: $310,000.
- Median staffing for parallel SB 53 and RAISE Act compliance: 6.5 full-time employees.
- Startups that delayed a California or New York launch in the past 12 months: 34%.
- Members citing conflicting state definitions as their top compliance issue: 61%.

A bill that removed the state patchwork and added no federal safety apparatus would cut most of those numbers at a stroke. A bill that did both would leave the industry worse off than the status quo, and we would be obliged to say so.

ACIA appreciates the seriousness of this draft and the openness to revision that the discussion-draft process reflects. Preemption of state model-development law is hard, bipartisan, and overdue; we want to help you get it right and make it durable. We stand ready to provide technical assistance, section-by-section markup suggestions, and member briefings as the committee prepares introduced text.

Respectfully submitted,

**Grant Holloway**
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance
Washington, DC

# DRAFT for ACIA policy review

# One national standard, not a federal safety bureau

## ACIA's asks on the Great American AI Act (GAAIA) discussion draft

*For House Energy & Commerce offices. From the American Compute & Innovation Alliance, a Washington, DC coalition of about 140 AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, semiconductor startups, and venture firms. Contact: Tessa Marchetti, VP Policy.*

**The position in one line:** GAAIA's federal preemption of state model-development law is the most valuable AI action Congress can take. Make it permanent, and strip out the frontier-safety bureaucracy that rides along with it.

### Five asks

**1. Make Sec. 121 preemption permanent.** Strike the three-year sunset. A 2030 cliff re-fragments the market just as companies finish building to a single standard. Keep the savings clause as drafted: states retain authority over deployment, general-applicability laws, and common-law remedies.

**2. Strike the Sec. 111 incident-reporting mandate.** Under Sec. 101(7), any weight exfiltration, any tripped risk-mitigation control, or any claimed "loss of control" is reportable, with no requirement of actual harm, on 15-day and 24-hour clocks. Weight theft is already covered by computer-intrusion, trade-secret, and breach law. Median one-off cost to stand up a reporting function: $310,000.

**3. Strike Sec. 102, the CAISI codification and funding.** $100 million a year is roughly seven times CAISI's current ~$15 million appropriation, financed partly by fees on the developers it would police. Keep standards voluntary and industry-led, and return NIST to measurement science.

**4. Strike Sec. 112, the licensed-auditor (IVO) regime.** A small set of federally licensed auditors, paid by the companies they audit, with a mandatory referral trigger tied to "imminent" catastrophic risk, a term the draft leaves undefined, and penalties up to $1 million a day, is a recipe for regulatory capture.

**5. Keep and fund the build provisions.** Sec. 301 (Cybersecurity Act of 2015 reauthorization), Sec. 311 (critical open-source maintainers), Sec. 321 (model-weight security report), Sec. 401 (AI testbeds), NAIRR codification, and Sec. 122 (GAO report on regulatory impediments).

### Why it matters

ACIA's August 2026 member survey (86 respondents, self-selected) found: 61% call conflicting state definitions their top compliance problem; 34% of startups delayed a California or New York launch in the past year over state AI rules; parallel SB 53 and RAISE Act compliance takes a median of 6.5 full-time employees.

**Bottom line:** A permanent national standard without the safety bureaucracy is a bill ACIA can support and promote to our members. The bureaucracy without permanence is a bill we will oppose.

# Staff Q&A: anticipated questions on ACIA's GAAIA position

*DRAFT answers for ACIA staff, to be cleared by Tessa Marchetti, VP Policy, before external use. Keep each answer at or under 120 words in delivery.*

## 1. Majority E&C staff: "If you support preemption, why not incident reporting? It's lighter than SB 53."

Preemption and reporting do different work. Preemption deletes cost: it replaces SB 53, the RAISE Act and their imitators with one standard. Reporting adds a new federal mandate on top. And it is not lighter. SB 53 generally requires actual harm before an event is reportable; Sec. 101(7) of the draft counts any weight exfiltration, any tripped risk-mitigation control and any claimed "loss of control," harm or no harm, on 15-day and 24-hour clocks. The catastrophic-risk premise behind those terms is one our members consider unfounded. Weight theft is real and already covered by computer-intrusion and trade-secret law. Members put the stand-up cost of a reporting function at a $310,000 median, for no added safety.

## 2. Minority (Trahan-aligned) staff: "Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?"

Several, and the letter says so. We would accept a permanent national standard that displaces conflicting state development rules. We support NIST measurement science and voluntary, industry-led standards, on the AI Risk Management Framework model. We support procurement rules that reward demonstrated security and evaluation practices. We support the draft's Title III security items: funding for critical open-source maintainers (Sec. 311) and the model-weight security report (Sec. 321). And we accept enforcement against concrete harms through existing fraud, consumer-protection and computer-crime law, which Secs. 131 and 132 rightly reinforce. What we do not accept is mandatory reporting and a licensed auditor bureaucracy premised on speculative catastrophic risk.

## 3. Senate Commerce staff: "Three years or permanent? What's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?"

Permanent. A sunset treats the patchwork as a temporary irritant instead of the core problem, and it guarantees the fight returns: the Senate's 99-1 vote in July 2025 to strip the ten-year moratorium from the budget reconciliation shows preemption gets relitigated regardless. Our members build compliance infrastructure on multi-year cycles. A 2030 cliff strands half that investment and renegotiates the rest. Permanence is also the honest deal: Sec. 121 preserves state authority over deployment, general-applicability laws and common-law remedies, so the federal standard should be durable in exchange.

## 4. Appropriations staff: "CAISI is authorized at $100 million a year. What's your view on the funding level?"

Our position is no funding for a codified CAISI, and the letter asks appropriators directly to hold it flat or defund it. The draft authorizes $100 million a year, roughly seven times the current appropriation of about $15 million, plus fee authority over licensed auditors and large frontier developers. That is a regulator sized for a risk we do not think is established, financed by the companies it polices. If Congress funds anything here, fund NIST's core measurement-science work, which the industry adopts voluntarily. We will repeat that request in the FY2027 and FY2028 appropriations cycles.
