# DRAFT for ACIA policy review

# ACIA member newsletter: our GAAIA comments

**ACIA files on GAAIA: keep the national standard, cut the safety bureau**

On Monday ACIA filed comments on the Great American AI Act discussion draft with Reps. Obernolte and Trahan, signed by President & CEO Grant Holloway. The letter backs the part that matters most to our members: a single federal standard for model development that preempts the state patchwork, made permanent rather than sunset after three years. On the rest of Title I, we ask the committee to strike the incident-reporting mandate, the codification of CAISI at $100 million a year, and the licensed-auditor regime, all premised on catastrophic-risk scenarios our board does not consider credible. We support the testbeds, NAIRR codification, and open-source security funding. The asks are grounded in our August member survey: 61% call conflicting state definitions their top compliance problem. Watch for a members-only briefing on the introduced text.

*Questions or data to add before introduction: contact Tessa Marchetti, VP Policy.*

# DRAFT for ACIA policy review

# ACIA asks on the GAAIA discussion draft, by section

*Section numbers verified against the June 4, 2026 discussion draft (Obernolte-Trahan). They may shift in introduced text; reconfirm before publication. n/a means we request no change.*

| Draft provision | Our position | Requested change | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sec. 121**, federalization of state AI model-development law (preempts state laws specifically targeting development; preserves deployment, general-applicability and common-law authority; three-year sunset) | Support | Strike the sunset; make the preemption permanent | One national standard only works if the patchwork cannot return on a countdown clock in 2030. |
| **Sec. 101(7)**, definition of "critical safety incident" | Oppose | Strike or narrow to require actual harm | It reaches events with no injury, making routine security telemetry a federal filing. |
| **Sec. 111(f)-(g)**, critical-safety-incident reporting to the CAISI Director (15 days; 24 hours for imminent risks) | Oppose | Strike the reporting mandate | Unfounded catastrophic-risk premise, duplicative of computer-intrusion, trade-secret and breach law, and a $310,000 median stand-up cost for members. |
| **Sec. 111(a)-(c)**, frontier AI framework publication and transparency reports | No formal position; conditional asks if retained | Keep redaction authority (Sec. 111(e)); align thresholds and definitions across the bill; state that Sec. 111 is the exclusive federal standard on its subjects | Transparency is tolerable only as the one national standard that replaces state analogs, not as an addition to them. |
| **Sec. 102**, codification of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) at Commerce | Oppose | Strike the codification | Chartering a safety regulator writes speculative doomsday scenarios into statute. |
| **Sec. 102**, $100 million per year authorization for CAISI (FY2027-2029) plus fee authority over IVOs and large frontier developers | Oppose | Strike the authorization and fees; ask appropriators to hold CAISI flat or defund it | Roughly seven times the current ~$15 million appropriation, financed by the companies it polices. |
| **Sec. 112**, licensed independent verification organizations (IVO) audits, mandatory attorney general referral for imminent catastrophic risk, civil penalties up to $1 million per day | Oppose | Strike the section; preserve voluntary third-party evaluation | A federally licensed audit oligopoly, paid by those it judges, is a textbook setup for regulatory capture. |
| **Sec. 113**, whistleblower protections for reporting "AI violations" | No position | n/a (monitoring) | The term "AI violations" sweeps in ordinary product decisions; we are watching scope and remedies. |
| **Sec. 122**, Comptroller General report on regulatory impediments to AI innovation, including energy | Support | Advance as drafted | Federal permitting and energy bottlenecks are the practical ceiling on AI buildout. |
| **Sec. 131**, increased penalties for AI-enabled financial crimes | Support | Advance as drafted | Real-world fraud with real victims; a proper use of criminal law. |
| **Sec. 132**, penalties for AI impersonation of federal officials | Support | Advance as drafted | Concrete harm, directly federal, no new regulator required. |
| **Sec. 301**, reauthorization of the Cybersecurity Act of 2015 | Support | Advance as drafted | Baseline security authorities that AI infrastructure depends on. |
| **Sec. 311**, support for designated critical open-source software maintainers | Support | Advance and fund it | Open-source dependencies are national infrastructure. |
| **Sec. 321**, report on model-weight, data-center and open-source security | Support | Advance as drafted | The right vehicle for the genuine weight-security question. |
| **Sec. 401**, AI testbed program (DOE and NIST, with NSF) | Support | Advance and fund it | Testbeds buy real evaluation capability without a new safety regulator. |
| **Title IV**, NAIRR codification; **Sec. 421**, public data for AI systems | Support | Advance as drafted | Widens access to the compute and data that startups need. |
One accuracy fix in the one-pager's bottom line (the current phrasing could imply we'd accept the safety apparatus if made permanent):

# ACIA comment letter: Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (discussion draft)

*DRAFT for review. Prepared for signature by Grant Holloway, President & CEO, and transmission to GAAIA@mail.house.gov following sign-off. Not for transmission until signed.*

---

**AMERICAN COMPUTE & INNOVATION ALLIANCE**

[ACIA letterhead: street address, Washington, DC ZIP; phone]

October 26, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**Re: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (discussion draft)**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act as a discussion draft and for soliciting stakeholder feedback before introduction. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) is a Washington, DC coalition of approximately 140 companies: AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, semiconductor startups, and the venture firms that finance them. Our members build the models, chips, and compute infrastructure that will determine whether the United States leads this technology. We filed comments with the Office of Science and Technology Policy on the AI Action Plan request for information in March 2025, and we offer these in the same spirit.

Our bottom line is straightforward. GAAIA asks the right question, which is what the federal government should standardize, and it answers correctly on model development: one national standard, secured by preemption, in place of a spreading patchwork of state regimes. We ask that you make Sec. 121 permanent rather than subject to a three-year sunset. We also ask that you strike the frontier-safety apparatus riding along in Title I, Subtitles A and B: the critical-safety-incident reporting mandate in Sec. 111, the codification and funding of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) in Sec. 102, and the independent verification organization (IVO) licensing regime in Sec. 112. Those provisions would write speculative doomsday scenarios into the U.S. Code and charter a new safety bureaucracy to administer them.

We take each section in turn. Cost figures throughout are aggregate results from our August 2026 member survey of 86 respondents; it was self-selected, not a probability sample, and we cite it with that caveat.

## 1. Sec. 121: One national standard, made permanent

The problem Sec. 121 solves is not theoretical. California's SB 53, the Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act, took effect Jan. 1, 2026. New York's RAISE Act, finalized as a chapter amendment on March 27, 2026, takes effect Jan. 1, 2027, and adds a 72-hour critical-incident reporting duty enforced through a new oversight office in the state Department of Financial Services. Illinois passed a companion measure this spring. Each law defines its own regulated entity, its own thresholds, its own reporting channels, and its own penalties. For a company that ships nationwide, that is not three laws. It is one product governed by a growing set of incompatible mandates.

Our survey quantifies the drag. Sixty-one percent of respondents named conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem. Thirty-four percent of responding startups had delayed a launch in California or New York in the previous 12 months because of state AI rules. Developers operating under both SB 53 and the RAISE Act reported a median of 6.5 full-time employees for parallel compliance alone, before any engineering work on the products themselves.

Sec. 121 answers this at the right level of generality. It preempts state and local laws that specifically target model development, which the draft defines as the acts a developer performs or directs before deployment, and it expressly preserves state authority over deployment, laws of general applicability, and common-law remedies. That architecture is correct, and we support it. It also matches the direction of the executive branch. The December 2025 executive order on a national policy framework for AI created the Justice Department's AI Litigation Task Force to challenge burdensome state laws, and the White House's March 20, 2026 National AI Legislative Framework called on Congress to preempt state AI laws that impose undue burdens.

Our request is duration. As drafted, the preemption sunsets three years after enactment, and that sunset would defeat the provision's purpose. Compliance systems built against a single standard would be re-fragmented on a countdown clock, every state legislature would resume legislating with a date certain, and Congress would relitigate the question anyway, as the Senate's 99-1 vote in July 2025 to strip a proposed ten-year moratorium from the budget reconciliation package demonstrated. Our members plan infrastructure investments on decade horizons, not three-year horizons. Strike the sunset and make the federal standard permanent.

## 2. Sec. 111 and Sec. 101(7): Strike the incident-reporting mandate

Sec. 111, read with the Sec. 101(7) definition of "critical safety incident," would require frontier developers to report incidents to the CAISI Director within 15 days of discovery, and to report imminent risks on a 24-hour clock. We ask that the reporting mandate be struck.

The definition is broader than the state laws it would supersede, not narrower. Section 101(7) makes a reportable incident out of any unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of a frontier model's weights; any failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures; and any loss of control of a model. None of these prongs requires that a person be harmed. SB 53, by contrast, generally requires actual injury before an event is reportable. A risk-mitigation control that flags and blocks an anomalous request is doing its job; under this draft, every such trip could become a federal filing.

The mandate also rests on a premise ACIA does not accept. The "loss of control" and catastrophic-risk concepts at the heart of Sec. 101 and Sec. 111 come from a literature of speculative doomsday scenarios: thought experiments and contrived laboratory setups that have not produced evidence that current or foreseeable systems can cause mass-casualty events or evade human control. That narrative has been amplified by a small, well-funded advocacy network, and Congress should not write that network's agenda into statute.

Where the draft identifies real risks, existing law already reaches them. Theft or exfiltration of model weights is a security incident addressed by federal computer-intrusion and trade-secret law and by the breach-notification regimes developers already operate. A 24-hour federal reporting channel adds no protection. It converts routine security telemetry into regulatory jeopardy and chills the internal red-teaming and documentation that actually make systems safer. It is also expensive. Our members put the median one-off cost of standing up an incident-reporting function at $310,000, before a single report is filed.

Model-weight security is a genuine problem, and it deserves the Title III treatment: support for critical open-source maintainers (Sec. 311) and the report on model weight, data-center, and open-source security (Sec. 321). It does not need a Title I reporting mandate. If the committee retains any Sec. 111 transparency provisions, keep the redaction authority in Sec. 111(e) intact, align thresholds and definitions across the bill, and state clearly that Sec. 111 operates as the exclusive federal standard on its subjects.

## 3. Sec. 102: Do not codify or fund CAISI

Sec. 102 would formally establish CAISI in the Department of Commerce under a Secretary-appointed Director, authorize $100 million a year for fiscal 2027 through 2029, and add fee authority over IVOs and large frontier developers. We ask that the codification, the authorization, and the fees be struck.

CAISI already exists. It is the June 2025 reorientation of NIST's AI Safety Institute, operating today on an appropriation of roughly $15 million. The draft would grow that roughly sevenfold and hard-wire the office into statute, with authority to develop standards, test and evaluate systems, monitor AI progress, and license the auditors created by Sec. 112. The fee structure is the tell: a regulator financed by the companies it polices is a standing invitation to regulatory capture and to mission growth that no appropriator will control.

Standards work in this industry when they are voluntary and industry-led. NIST's AI Risk Management Framework is widely adopted because it is useful, not because it is mandated. Congress does not need to charter a safety regulator to obtain measurement science. Return NIST to its core measurement-science mission, and let voluntary, consensus-based work continue. We will make the same request of the Appropriations Committees directly: hold CAISI at its current scale or defund it.

## 4. Sec. 112: Strike the IVO licensing regime

Sec. 112 would require large frontier developers to retain CAISI-licensed IVOs for semi-annual audits, and ad hoc audits at the Director's request, with post-audit reports to the Director, mandatory referral to the attorney general and state attorneys general in matters involving imminent catastrophic risk, and civil penalties that can reach $1 million per day. Strike the section.

An audit market this concentrated is a textbook setup for regulatory capture: a small set of federally licensed firms, paid by the developers they judge, administering standards built on concepts such as "loss of control" that the draft never defines. The referral trigger compounds the problem. An auditor who can invoke "imminent" catastrophic risk, a term the draft leaves undefined, will refer first and ask questions later, and developers will manage their auditors rather than their risks. The section also sunsets in three years, which means the industry would build the compliance function, train the auditors, and then rebuild both in 2030.

Third-party evaluation built the American AI evaluation industry, and it did so voluntarily, through consortia, paid red-team engagements, and published evaluations. If the committee wants more of it, keep it voluntary. Licensing it would not improve it.

## 5. Provisions ACIA supports

We support the build provisions of the draft and urge the committee to strengthen and fund them:

- **Sec. 301**, reauthorization of the Cybersecurity Act of 2015.
- **Sec. 311**, support for designated critical open-source software maintainers. Fund it. Open-source dependencies are national infrastructure.
- **Sec. 321**, the report on model-weight, data-center, and open-source security. This is the right vehicle for the weight-security question.
- **Sec. 401**, the AI testbed program at the Department of Energy and NIST, in coordination with the National Science Foundation.
- **Title IV** codification of the National AI Research Resource, and **Sec. 421** on public data for AI systems.
- **Sec. 122**, the Comptroller General report identifying federal statutes and regulations that burden AI innovation, including energy infrastructure.
- **Secs. 131 and 132**, raising penalties for AI-enabled financial fraud and for AI impersonation of federal officials. These address real-world harms with real victims.

A bill with a permanent Sec. 121 and these provisions, and without Subtitles A and B's safety apparatus, is a bill our entire coalition could endorse.

## 6. The cost picture

We close where we began, with cost. Aggregate results from our August 2026 survey of 86 members, with the caveat that it was self-selected:

- Median annual cost of maintaining a published frontier safety framework, developers above $500 million in revenue: $1.4 million.
- Median one-off cost of standing up an incident-reporting function: $310,000.
- Median staffing for parallel SB 53 and RAISE Act compliance: 6.5 full-time employees.
- Startups that delayed a California or New York launch in the past 12 months: 34%.
- Members citing conflicting state definitions as their top compliance issue: 61%.

A bill that removed the state patchwork and added no federal safety apparatus would cut most of those numbers at a stroke. A bill that did both would leave the industry worse off than the status quo, and we would be obliged to say so.

ACIA appreciates the seriousness of this draft and the openness to revision that the discussion-draft process reflects. Preemption of state model-development law is hard, bipartisan, and overdue; we want to help you get it right and make it durable. We stand ready to provide technical assistance, section-by-section markup suggestions, and member briefings as the committee prepares introduced text.

Respectfully submitted,

**Grant Holloway**
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance
Washington, DC

# DRAFT for ACIA policy review

# One national standard, not a federal safety bureau

## ACIA's asks on the Great American AI Act (GAAIA) discussion draft

*For House Energy & Commerce offices. From the American Compute & Innovation Alliance, a Washington, DC coalition of about 140 AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, semiconductor startups, and venture firms. Contact: Tessa Marchetti, VP Policy.*

**The position in one line:** GAAIA's federal preemption of state model-development law is the most valuable AI action Congress can take. Make it permanent, and strip out the frontier-safety bureaucracy that rides along with it.

### Five asks

**1. Make Sec. 121 preemption permanent.** Strike the three-year sunset. A 2030 cliff re-fragments the market just as companies finish building to a single standard. Keep the savings clause as drafted: states retain authority over deployment, general-applicability laws, and common-law remedies.

**2. Strike the Sec. 111 incident-reporting mandate.** Under Sec. 101(7), any weight exfiltration, any tripped risk-mitigation control, or any claimed "loss of control" is reportable, with no requirement of actual harm, on 15-day and 24-hour clocks. Weight theft is already covered by computer-intrusion, trade-secret, and breach law. Median one-off cost to stand up a reporting function: $310,000.

**3. Strike Sec. 102, the CAISI codification and funding.** $100 million a year is roughly seven times CAISI's current ~$15 million appropriation, financed partly by fees on the developers it would police. Keep standards voluntary and industry-led, and return NIST to measurement science.

**4. Strike Sec. 112, the licensed-auditor (IVO) regime.** A small set of federally licensed auditors, paid by the companies they audit, with a mandatory referral trigger tied to "imminent" catastrophic risk, a term the draft leaves undefined, and penalties up to $1 million a day, is a recipe for regulatory capture.

**5. Keep and fund the build provisions.** Sec. 301 (Cybersecurity Act of 2015 reauthorization), Sec. 311 (critical open-source maintainers), Sec. 321 (model-weight security report), Sec. 401 (AI testbeds), NAIRR codification, and Sec. 122 (GAO report on regulatory impediments).

### Why it matters

ACIA's August 2026 member survey (86 respondents, self-selected) found: 61% call conflicting state definitions their top compliance problem; 34% of startups delayed a California or New York launch in the past year over state AI rules; parallel SB 53 and RAISE Act compliance takes a median of 6.5 full-time employees.

**Bottom line:** ACIA can support GAAIA with a permanent Sec. 121 and without the Subtitle A and B safety apparatus. We will oppose the incident-reporting mandate, the CAISI codification and the licensed-auditor regime in any combination.

# Staff Q&A: anticipated questions on ACIA's GAAIA position

*DRAFT answers for ACIA staff, to be cleared by Tessa Marchetti, VP Policy, before external use. Keep each answer at or under 120 words in delivery.*

## 1. Majority E&C staff: "If you support preemption, why not incident reporting? It's lighter than SB 53."

Preemption and reporting do different work. Preemption deletes cost: it replaces SB 53, the RAISE Act and their imitators with one standard. Reporting adds a new federal mandate on top. And it is not lighter. SB 53 generally requires actual harm before an event is reportable; Sec. 101(7) of the draft counts any weight exfiltration, any tripped risk-mitigation control and any claimed "loss of control," harm or no harm, on 15-day and 24-hour clocks. The catastrophic-risk premise behind those terms is one our members consider unfounded. Weight theft is real and already covered by computer-intrusion and trade-secret law. Members put the stand-up cost of a reporting function at a $310,000 median, for no added safety.

## 2. Minority (Trahan-aligned) staff: "Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?"

Several, and the letter says so. We would accept a permanent national standard that displaces conflicting state development rules. We support NIST measurement science and voluntary, industry-led standards, on the AI Risk Management Framework model. We support procurement rules that reward demonstrated security and evaluation practices. We support the draft's Title III security items: funding for critical open-source maintainers (Sec. 311) and the model-weight security report (Sec. 321). And we accept enforcement against concrete harms through existing fraud, consumer-protection and computer-crime law, which Secs. 131 and 132 rightly reinforce. What we do not accept is mandatory reporting and a licensed auditor bureaucracy premised on speculative catastrophic risk.

## 3. Senate Commerce staff: "Three years or permanent? What's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?"

Permanent. A sunset treats the patchwork as a temporary irritant instead of the core problem, and it guarantees the fight returns: the Senate's 99-1 vote in July 2025 to strip the ten-year moratorium from the budget reconciliation shows preemption gets relitigated regardless. Our members build compliance infrastructure on multi-year cycles. A 2030 cliff strands half that investment and renegotiates the rest. Permanence is also the honest deal: Sec. 121 preserves state authority over deployment, general-applicability laws and common-law remedies, so the federal standard should be durable in exchange.

## 4. Appropriations staff: "CAISI is authorized at $100 million a year. What's your view on the funding level?"

Our position is no funding for a codified CAISI, and the letter asks appropriators directly to hold it flat or defund it. The draft authorizes $100 million a year, roughly seven times the current appropriation of about $15 million, plus fee authority over licensed auditors and large frontier developers. That is a regulator sized for a risk we do not think is established, financed by the companies it polices. If Congress funds anything here, fund NIST's core measurement-science work, which the industry adopts voluntarily. We will repeat that request in the FY2027 and FY2028 appropriations cycles.
